title: Binary shift and hexadecimal
starter: Why might a programmer prefer to write FF rather than 11111111? Suggest two reasons.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Left shift
facts: Every bit moves left, and a 0 comes in at the right.
A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
Any bit pushed off the left end is lost: that's an overflow.
stations.challenge: Illustrate a left shift of 1 on an 8-bit number without an overflow.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Every bit moves left, and a 0 comes in at the right.
Also credit: A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.

questions.q: Shift this number one place to the left.
What does a left shift of 2 places do to a number?

stations.name: Right shift
facts: Every bit moves right, and a 0 comes in at the left.
A shift of one place divides the number by 2.
Bits pushed off the right end are lost, so the answer is rounded down.
stations.challenge: Illustrate a right shift of 1 on an 8-bit number without an underflow.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Every bit moves right, and a 0 comes in at the left.
Also credit: A shift of one place divides the number by 2.

questions.q: Shift this number one place to the right.
What happens when a 1 is pushed off the right-hand end during a right shift?
questions.a: It is lost, so the answer is rounded down

stations.name: Shifts and precision
facts: Shifting is very fast, so processors use it instead of multiplying and dividing where they can.
Left shifts can overflow if a 1 is pushed off the left end.
stations.challenge: Why might a programmer use a shift instead of multiplying by 2?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Shifting is very fast, so processors use it instead of multiplying and dividing where they can.
Also credit: Left shifts can overflow if a 1 is pushed off the left end.

questions.q: Shift this number two places to the left.
Why do processors use shifts rather than multiplication where possible?
questions.a: A shift is a much faster operation

stations.name: Why hexadecimal?
facts: Hexadecimal is base 16, using 0-9 then A-F.
One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits.
It's much shorter and easier for people to read and copy than long binary.
stations.challenge: Write out the hex digits and their denary values.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Hexadecimal is base 16, using 0-9 then A-F.
Also credit: One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits.

questions.a: It is shorter than binary and easier to read, and each digit is exactly 4 bits

questions.q: What is the denary value of the hex digit C?

stations.name: Denary and hex
facts: Denary to hex: divide by 16; the whole number is the first digit, the remainder the second.
Or convert to binary first, then split into two nibbles.
Hex to denary: first digit × 16, plus the second digit.
stations.challenge: Convert 207 into hexadecimal, showing your method.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Denary to hex: divide by 16; the whole number is the first digit, the remainder the second.
Also credit: Or convert to binary first, then split into two nibbles.

stations.name: Binary and hex
facts: Split the byte into two nibbles of 4 bits.
Convert each nibble separately into one hex digit.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Split the byte into two nibbles of 4 bits.
Also credit: Convert each nibble separately into one hex digit.

exam.q: Explain what a left shift of one place achieves.
points: A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
A shift of one place divides the number by 2.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Perform a right shift of two places on 10110000 and state the denary result.
points: A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
Every bit moves left, and a 0 comes in at the right.
Every bit moves right, and a 0 comes in at the left.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Convert the denary number 207 into hexadecimal.
points: Denary to hex: divide by 16; the whole number is the first digit, the remainder the second.
A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Convert the binary number 10111010 into hexadecimal.
points: Or convert to binary first, then split into two nibbles.
A shift of one place multiplies the number by 2; two places multiplies by 4.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
